questions.q: Is freezing water into ice a reversible or an irreversible change?
questions.a: It is a reversible change. A wrong answer suggests the student confuses "hardened" states (like ice) with permanent changes; explain that heating ice simply turns it back to water, proving it is the same substance.

questions.q: If you bake a clay pot in a kiln, why is it considered an irreversible change?
questions.a: It is irreversible because the heat causes a permanent change in the material, and you cannot turn the hardened pot back into soft, moldable clay. A wrong answer shows the student ignores the "new substance" or "permanent state" aspect of the change.

questions.q: A rubber band is stretched and then released. Why is this a reversible change?
questions.a: It is reversible because the rubber band returns to its original shape and size once the pulling force is removed. A wrong answer indicates the student thinks any change in shape (even temporary) is irreversible.

questions.q: Compare burning a candle to melting a candle. Which is reversible, and which is not?
questions.a: Melting is reversible (you can collect and re-freeze the wax), but burning is irreversible (the wax turns into smoke and ash). A wrong answer reveals the student focuses on the "wax" material only, ignoring the chemical consumption during burning.

questions.q: If you mix salt and water, can you recover the salt? If so, is the process reversible?
questions.a: Yes, it is reversible; you can recover the salt by evaporating the water. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks "dissolving" means the salt has disappeared or turned into a new substance.

questions.q: Think of a change in your kitchen that is irreversible. Explain why you cannot undo it.
questions.a: Cooking vegetables is a classic example because the heat permanently changes the structure and color of the food. A poor answer fails to explain *why* (e.g., just saying "it's done" without mentioning the inability to revert).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A reversible change is one that can be undone to restore the original substance, whereas an ______ change creates a new substance or condition that cannot be returned to its previous state.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever wondered why you can turn ice back into ______, but you can’t turn a cooked omelet back into a raw egg?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to categorize a list of everyday actions as reversible or irreversible and provide a logical reason for their classification based on whether the original material can be recovered.
